artiest/huelgas-ensemble-en-paul-van-nev.text:
The Huelgas Ensemble is a Belgian early-music group, founded in 1971 by the Flemish conductor Paul Van Nevel. Its name refers to a manuscript of polyphonic music, the Codex Las Huelgas. The ensemble concentrates on Renaissance polyphony, and has built up an extensive discography of it.

Van Nevel is known for his own way of working. For many pieces he has the singers and himself stand in a large circle around a microphone hanging above the centre. For concerts in 2005 at the Rheingau Musik Festival, the pews in the basilica of Schloss Johannisberg even had to be unscrewed from the floor. In 2009, after eight years with Harmonia Mundi, the group returned to Sony Classical, which reissued a box set of fifteen CDs.

The group is important above all for the way it makes the polyphony of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries audible: each voice is an independent line, and together they form a rich and clear whole. Nuper rosarum flores by Guillaume Dufay from 1436, a motet for the consecration of the dome of Florence Cathedral, is an example of this music. Such recordings also made early music accessible to listeners who come from pop.
artiest/huelgas-ensemble-en-paul-van-nev.listen: Listen to Nuper rosarum flores and notice how the voices take turns in the lead. Try to tell the low, slowly moving voices apart from the ornamented melody on top.

artiest/hugh-masekela.text: Hugh Masekela grew up near Johannesburg. As a teenager he was given a trumpet that had belonged to Louis Armstrong, courtesy of the priest Trevor Huddleston, and Armstrong became his great example. In 1959 he played in The Jazz Epistles. In 1960 he left South Africa and studied in London and New York, helped by Harry Belafonte and Miriam Makeba, whom he married. In 1968 Grazing in the Grass topped the American chart. His music blended jazz with mbaqanga and African pop. Stimela is about miners travelling by train to the gold mines. After the end of apartheid he returned to South Africa in 1990.
artiest/hugh-masekela.listen: Listen to the warm, singing trumpet above an African rhythm.

artiest/hugh-padgham.text:
Hugh Padgham is an English record producer and sound engineer, born on 15 February 1955 in Amersham, Buckinghamshire. He became interested in production after listening to Tumbleweed Connection by Elton John. He began as a tape operator at Advision Studios, where he worked on recordings by Mott the Hoople and Gentle Giant, among others, and then became an engineer at Lansdowne Studios. In 1978 he got a job at The Townhouse, where he worked with XTC, Peter Gabriel and Phil Collins. He was also involved in the second album by Killing Joke.

His work with Gabriel and Collins led in the 1980s to a collaboration with Genesis and Collins, on albums such as Face Value and Abacab from 1981, Genesis from 1983, No Jacket Required from 1985 and Invisible Touch from 1986. With The Police he co-produced Ghost in the Machine from 1981 and Synchronicity from 1983, and later he worked on material by Sting, on Press to Play by Paul McCartney and on Hysteria by the Human League from 1984. In the 2000s he produced McFly, with four number ones in the United Kingdom in 2005 and 2006.

Padgham won four Grammys. He is regarded as one of the creators of the gated reverb drum sound, heard above all on In the Air Tonight by Phil Collins from 1981, which became the template for much of the pop drum sound of the 1980s. In 2019 he received an award in London for his contribution to British music.
artiest/hugh-padgham.listen: Listen to In the Air Tonight by Phil Collins. Notice the moment the drums come in and how the reverb is abruptly cut off: that is the gated reverb.

artiest/hugh-wolff.text:
Hugh Wolff is an American conductor, born on 21 October 1953 in Neuilly-sur-Seine in France, where his father worked for the American foreign service. He spent his primary-school years in London. He studied at Harvard and at the Peabody Conservatory. Between the two he spent a year in Paris, studying composition with Olivier Messiaen and conducting with Charles Bruck. At the Peabody he took piano lessons from Leon Fleisher.

In 1979 he began as an assistant to Mstislav Rostropovich at the National Symphony Orchestra in Washington. In 1985 he was the first winner of the Seaver/National Endowment for the Arts Conductors Award. He was music director of the New Jersey Symphony Orchestra from 1986 to 1993 and led the Saint Paul Chamber Orchestra, first as principal conductor from 1988 and from 1992 to 2000 as music director. From 1997 to 2006 he was chief conductor of the Frankfurt Radio Symphony, and from 2017 of the Belgian National Orchestra.

Wolff made many recordings for Teldec and Sony, among others, received three Grammy nominations and twice won the Cannes Classical Award. His discography includes all of Beethoven's symphonies with the Frankfurt orchestra. He accompanied recordings by Rostropovich, Yo-Yo Ma, Joshua Bell, Hilary Hahn, Dawn Upshaw and the jazz guitarist John Scofield. He teaches at the New England Conservatory in Boston. His work shows how a conductor from the classical world can also collaborate in other genres.
artiest/hugh-wolff.listen: Listen to Appalachian Spring in Copland's original chamber version, conducted by Wolff. Notice how transparent the small ensemble sounds and how you can follow every instrument.

artiest/hugo-friedhofer.text:
Hugo Friedhofer was an American composer and cellist, known for his film music. He was born on 3 May 1901 in San Francisco and died on 17 May 1981. His father was a cello teacher who had studied in Dresden, and his mother was born in Germany. He began playing the cello at thirteen, took lessons in harmony and counterpoint at the University of California in Berkeley and played in the People's Symphony Orchestra.

In 1929 he moved to Hollywood, where he worked as a musician for Fox, including on Sunny Side Up. Later he became an orchestrator at Warner Bros. and worked on more than fifty films. There he worked mainly with Max Steiner and, because he spoke German, with Erich Wolfgang Korngold. Steiner relied on his ability to turn sketches into a full orchestral score. In 1937 he wrote his first film score of his own, for The Adventures of Marco Polo. In 1946 he composed the music for The Best Years of Our Lives by William Wyler, which won him the Oscar for best original score. He was nominated for eight other films, including The Bishop's Wife, Joan of Arc, Boy on a Dolphin and An Affair to Remember.

Colleagues admired him, and he was known for his biting, self-mocking humour. He belongs to the generation that shaped the orchestral sound of the Hollywood film. His work can be heard on records such as An Affair to Remember from 1957 and One Eyed Jacks from 1961.
artiest/hugo-friedhofer.listen: Listen to the main title of The Best Years of Our Lives. Notice the broad, calm melody that conveys something of coming home after the war.

artiest/husayn-isma-il-al-a-zami-en-ense.text:
Husayn Ismâ'îl al-A'zamî is a singer from Iraq who performs the classical vocal tradition of his country, the Iraqi maqam. He sings together with Ensemble Al-Kindî, a French group that plays classical Arabic music. The ensemble is named after al-Kindi, the ninth-century Arab philosopher and music theorist.

In Arabic music a maqam is more than a scale. It is a system of melodic rules and moods, within which the musician improvises. In the Iraqi tradition the soloist sings long, ornamented lines to old poems, accompanied by a small ensemble with instruments such as the lute (oud), the zither (qanun) and the violin or flute, and with percussion. The 1994 recording Maqâm Sabâ et pasta follows that model: a freely sung maqam Sabâ, followed by a pasta, a lighter, rhythmic song.

For the history of pop this music is important because it shows how far melody and improvisation can go without chords. The Arabic mode Sabâ has small intervals that do not exist in the Western system of twelve semitones. Anyone who hears these recordings understands why many pop musicians later began listening to such traditions. Little is documented here about the singer's life.
artiest/husayn-isma-il-al-a-zami-en-ense.listen: Listen to Maqâm Sabâ et pasta and pay attention to the voice: how does the singer glide between the notes, and what changes when a fixed rhythm sets in after the free opening?

artiest/huub-van-der-lubbe.text:
Huub van der Lubbe is a Dutch singer, poet and actor, born in 1953 in Amsterdam. In 1981 he played with his brother Hans in the rock 'n' roll band Big Shot and his Rocking Guns, which played songs in English. At the same time the brothers started the band De Dijk with Nico Arzbach, Pim Kops and Antonie Broek. The name came from the Zeedijk, a street in their home city of Amsterdam.

De Dijk mixed soul, blues and rock 'n' roll, with horns on stage and lyrics that were almost always in Dutch. Van der Lubbe wrote those lyrics himself. At the end of 1988 Niemand in de stad appeared, the band's most successful album. In 2010 De Dijk made the album Hold On Tight with the American soul singer Solomon Burke, who sang in English. In 1995 Van der Lubbe's song lyrics were collected as Melkboer met de blues, followed by volumes of poetry such as Geregeld leven (2003). He also acted in films, such as De aanslag (1986), and sang the Dutch-language songs in Toy Story.

De Dijk arose at the time when Dutch-language pop became big, with bands such as Doe Maar and Het Goede Doel. Because Van der Lubbe was also a poet and actor, the band appealed not only to teenagers but to people of all ages. A new generation of bands, such as Van Dik Hout and Bløf, named De Dijk as a major influence. In 2022 Van der Lubbe left the band, which then stopped. In 2017 he received the Lennaert Nijgh Prize.
artiest/huub-van-der-lubbe.listen: Listen to a song from De Dijk's album Niemand in de stad (1988). Notice how the soul and blues with horns go together with a Dutch lyric about the city.

artiest/huun-huur-tu.text:
Huun-Huur-Tu is a music group from Tuva, a republic in Russia on the border with Mongolia. The group is known for throat singing, in which a singer produces a fundamental note and overtones at the same time, so that two or three notes sound at once. The overtone can sound like a flute, a whistle or a bird, but comes entirely from the voice.

The ensemble began in 1992 as the khöömei quartet Kunggurtug, founded by Kaigal-ool Khovalyg, the brothers Alexander and Sayan Bapa, and Albert Kuvezin. Soon afterwards the name changed to Huun-Huur-Tu, which means sunbeams. The first album, 60 Horses In My Herd, appeared in 1993, followed by The Orphan's Lament (1994), If I'd Been Born An Eagle (1997) and Where Young Grass Grows (1999). Kuvezin left to start the rock group Yat-Kha.

The group plays traditional Tuvan songs, often about the steppe and horses, on instruments such as the igil, the khomus, the doshpuluur and the shaman drum dünggür. Later it carefully added Western instruments and electronics. Huun-Huur-Tu collaborated with Frank Zappa, the Kodo drummers, the Kronos Quartet, The Chieftains and Carmen Rizzo, among others. In this way the group brought throat singing to a worldwide audience and showed that pop music can also contain a different vocal technique.
artiest/huun-huur-tu.listen: Listen to Kongurei and try to hear two layers in the singing: a low, droning fundamental and above it a clear, whistling overtone.

artiest/hyderabad-brothers.text:
The Hyderabad Brothers were a Carnatic vocal duo: D. Raghavachari, born in 1952, and D. Seshachari, born in 1956 and died of cancer on 24 February 2024. They were among the most popular duet singers in South Indian classical music. Their name comes from their long association with the city of Hyderabad. Both came from a family of classical musicians. They received their first training from their father Daruri Ratnamacharyulu, and their mother Daruri Sulochana Devi was also a Carnatic singer. The brothers were born in Yakutpura. Raghavachari studied further with Susarla Sivaram at the Government College of Music and Dance in Hyderabad.

The duo performed in India for All India Radio and Doordarshan, among others, and in the United States, Canada, Australia and Qatar. At least fifty CDs and cassettes bear their name, including Scintillating Ragas from 1997. Seshachari was known for his powerful, deep and resonant singing, and Raghavachari for a softer, smoother voice. The two voices blend into a sound of their own, which fans compare to the Alathur Brothers.

Early in their career they received the award for best young talent in 1977 and 1978. The Madras Music Academy named them the best vocalists three years in a row, from 1990 to 1992, and in 1993 they received the Maharajapuram Viswanatha Iyer Award for the best performance of rare krithis by Thyagaraja. They passed on their knowledge to pupils, among them Ramesh Hariharan.
artiest/hyderabad-brothers.listen: Listen to Scintillating Ragas. Notice how the two voices alternate and complement each other, one deep and powerful, the other soft, and how together they build up the raga.

artiest/i-fiamminghi.text:
I Fiamminghi is a Belgian chamber orchestra from Brussels under the direction of the conductor Rudolf Werthen. Werthen is a violinist, conductor and teacher, born in Mechelen. He was taught by André Gertler and Henryk Szeryng. He founded the orchestra and is its artistic director. In 1989 he was also chief conductor of the symphony orchestra of the Flemish Opera. Since 1975 he has taught at the Royal Conservatoire of Ghent. In 1971 he was a laureate, with seventh prize for violin, at the Queen Elisabeth Competition, and in 1985 he sat on the violin jury.

The name literally means the Flemings and refers to the orchestra's Flemish origins. The discography runs from the Baroque to the present. Recordings include Le quattro stagioni in 1986, cello concertos in 1987 and 1994, Fratres in 1994 and Celestial Gate in 1995. Among the titles there are also newly written works, such as Creations, which shows that the orchestra plays both the standard repertoire and contemporary composers.

For the history of pop, I Fiamminghi is above all an orchestra that is often hired for recordings. That is typical of a chamber orchestra of this kind: it is small enough to be agile and large enough for a full string sound.
artiest/i-fiamminghi.listen: Listen to Fratres. Notice how the same simple sounds keep returning and slowly change colour.

artiest/i-wayan-lotring.text: I Wayan Lotring from Kuta, born around 1887, was one of the great innovators of Balinese gamelan. He learned the legong repertoire in Sukawati and in Kuta led a gamelan palégongan and a gendér wayang, which were recorded in 1928. In pieces such as Gambangan he built something new out of old forms. The Canadian composer Colin McPhee wrote that Lotring would wake at night to the new music in his head.
artiest/i-wayan-lotring.listen: Listen to Gambangan from 1928, with Lotring himself in the ensemble: the metallophones play interlocking patterns, so fast that they sound like one melody.

artiest/ian-curtis.text:
Ian Curtis was born on 15 July 1956 in Stretford and grew up in Macclesfield, near Manchester. He was a boy who loved reading, with a talent for poetry and an interest in philosophy and literature. Musically, Jim Morrison and David Bowie were his examples. After school he worked in a record shop and later as a civil servant.

In July 1976 he saw the Sex Pistols play in Manchester. There he met Bernard Sumner and Peter Hook, who wanted to start a band. Curtis offered himself as singer and lyricist, and in 1977 the drummer Stephen Morris joined. The band was first called Warsaw, after a Bowie song, and then Joy Division. Tony Wilson signed the group to his label Factory Records. Joy Division made two albums: Unknown Pleasures (1979) and Closer (1980). From the end of 1978 Curtis suffered from severe epilepsy, and he was troubled by depression. His jerky way of dancing on stage recalled his seizures. On 18 May 1980, just before the first American tour and before the release of Closer, he took his own life.

The three other members continued as New Order. Despite the short career, Joy Division's influence was great. It was one of the first post-punk bands to put atmosphere and expression ahead of anger and energy. In doing so the group pointed ahead to the melancholy alternative music of the 1980s, from The Cure and U2 to later bands such as Interpol and Editors. In 2026 Curtis was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame with Joy Division.
artiest/ian-curtis.listen: Listen to Love Will Tear Us Apart (1980). Notice Curtis's low, flat voice, which sings almost without emotion about a love that is falling apart, and the tight, driving rhythm of bass and drums beneath it.

artiest/ian-gillan.text:
Ian Gillan is an English singer, born in 1945 in Chiswick and raised in Hounslow, on the edge of London. As a boy he sang in a church choir and fell under the spell of Elvis Presley. In the mid-1960s he sang in local bands such as the Javelins and then in Episode Six. There he began writing songs with the bassist Roger Glover. In 1969 Deep Purple asked both of them to join the band, which wanted to move from psychedelic pop to hard rock.

With Deep Purple Gillan made In Rock (1970), Fireball, Machine Head and the live album Made in Japan. One of his first contributions was the melody and lyrics of Child in Time. Partly because of that song, Tim Rice asked him to sing Jesus on the original recording of Jesus Christ Superstar (1970). In 1973 he left the band, exhausted. After that he had the Ian Gillan Band, with a jazz-rock sound, and the heavier hard rock group Gillan. In 1983 he sang for a year with Black Sabbath on Born Again. From 1984 he sang with Deep Purple again, and since 1992 he has once more been its singer.

Gillan is known for his powerful voice with a large range, which can effortlessly go very high. He said that the singer Arthur Brown inspired him to start screaming in his singing. That combination of high wails and raw screams became a model for many singers in hard rock and heavy metal.
artiest/ian-gillan.listen: Listen to Child in Time (1970) by Deep Purple. Notice how Gillan starts quietly and lets his voice climb higher and higher, until he screams in his falsetto above Jon Lord's Hammond organ.

artiest/iannis-xenakis.text: Iannis Xenakis was badly wounded in the Greek Resistance and fled to Paris in 1947, where he went to work as an engineer for the architect Le Corbusier. He attended Messiaen's classes and began to calculate music with mathematics, probability theory and architecture. In Metastaseis from 1954, forty-six strings each glide separately up and down, in a cloud of sound that he drew as a graph. The same curved lines return in the Philips Pavilion at the 1958 World's Fair.
artiest/iannis-xenakis.listen: Listen to the beginning of Metastaseis and hear how all the strings start on one note and then each glide off in their own direction, until a broad cloud of sound forms.

artiest/ibrahim-al-mawsili.text:
Abu Ishaq Ibrahim al-Mawsili was an Arab musician of Persian descent, who lived from 742 to 804. He was among the greatest composers of the early Abbasid era. He was born in Kufa. His parents died early and an uncle directed his education. He went to Rayy, where he met an envoy of the caliph al-Mansur, who took him to Basra for singing lessons. Singing attracted him more than studying. At the age of twenty-three he fled to Mosul, where he joined a group of wild young men. His fame as a singer grew, and the caliph al-Mahdi brought him to court.

He served three caliphs in a row: al-Mahdi, al-Hadi and Harun al-Rashid. With the last he became especially close, and he became the foremost musician of his time. When he died, Harun had his son al-Ma'mun recite the prayer over the body. He defended the conservative school of Arabic music against innovators such as Ibn Jami. His son and pupil Ishaq al-Mawsili took over the leadership of that tradition. Other pupils were Mukhariq, the lutenist Zalzal and Ziryab. He appears in many stories from the One Thousand and One Nights.

He is known from traditions handed down, as in the Kitab al-Aghani. No recordings from his time exist; what you hear now is later music in his tradition.
artiest/ibrahim-al-mawsili.listen: Listen to a classical Arabic vocal improvisation with oud. Notice how the singer slowly spins out and ornaments a melody, as the court singers in Baghdad did.

artiest/ice-cube.text:
Ice Cube, who was born O'Shea Jackson on 15 June 1969 in Los Angeles, is an American rapper, songwriter, actor and film producer. He grew up in Westmont, in the south of the city. In his third year of high school he began writing raps, after a friend challenged him to in typing class. In 1986 he formed his first group, C.I.A., and in 1987 he founded the gangsta rap group N.W.A with Eazy-E and Dr. Dre. As the main rapper he wrote most of the lyrics of Straight Outta Compton from 1989, an album that shaped the early, violent and controversial identity of West Coast hip hop and distinguished it from that of the East Coast.

At the end of 1989 he left N.W.A after a money dispute over the group's management by Eazy-E and Jerry Heller. As a solo artist he made political rap albums: AmeriKKKa's Most Wanted from 1990, Death Certificate from 1991 and The Predator from 1992, all three of which were critical and commercial successes. His singles It Was a Good Day and Check Yo Self reached the top forty of the American Hot 100.

From the early 1990s he also made films. His first role was in Boyz n the Hood in 1991. He co-wrote the comedy Friday from 1995 and in 1998 directed The Players Club. In 2016 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame as a member of N.W.A.
artiest/ice-cube.listen: Listen to It Was a Good Day. Notice how calm and almost cheerful the beat sounds, and how over it Cube tells of an ordinary day in Los Angeles in his low, dry voice.

artiest/ice-t.text:
Ice-T, who was born Tracy Lauren Marrow on 16 February 1958 in Newark, New Jersey, is an American rapper and actor. He is active in both hip hop and heavy metal. He began in the 1980s as an underground rapper and signed to Sire Records in 1987, where his debut album Rhyme Pays was released. The following year he founded the label Rhyme $yndicate Records, named after his collective of hip hop artists, and released Power, his only album certified platinum by the RIAA. His subsequent albums, too, The Iceberg / Freedom of Speech… Just Watch What You Say from 1989, O.G. Original Gangster from 1991 and Home Invasion from 1993, received good reviews and gold status in the United States.

In 1990 he founded the metal band Body Count, which he introduced on O.G. Original Gangster. The band's debut album appeared in 1992. The song Cop Killer, which was about killing police officers, led to controversy. Ice-T asked to be released from his contract with Warner Bros. Records, and Home Invasion came out on Priority Records.

As an actor he played small parts in Breakin' and Rappin', and got his big role as Detective Scotty Appleton in New Jack City from 1991. Since 2000 he has played Sergeant Odafin Tutuola in Law & Order: Special Victims Unit, which made him the longest-running male actor in an American series. Ice-T is regarded as a pioneer of West Coast gangsta rap, and Body Count showed that rap and metal do not exclude each other.
artiest/ice-t.listen: Listen to Body Count on O.G. Original Gangster. Notice how the song combines rap, guitars and menacing lyrics, and what the move to metal does to his voice.

artiest/icp-orchestra.text:
The ICP Orchestra is the orchestra of the Instant Composers Pool, a Dutch collective for jazz and improvised music. The ICP label was founded in Amsterdam in 1967 by the saxophonist Willem Breuker, the pianist Misha Mengelberg and the drummer Han Bennink. The name refers to an idea of the founders: improvising is composing in the moment itself. European free jazz musicians then found it hard to get a record company, so they built a cooperative to release their own recordings.

Mengelberg and Bennink had been playing together since 1961 and in 1964 had contributed to the album Last Date by Eric Dolphy. Mengelberg came from the Fluxus movement and wrote compositions that work like games. Breuker left in 1974 to lead his own group, after which Mengelberg and Bennink extended their collaboration. In the 1970s the label also released records by Derek Bailey, Steve Lacy, Evan Parker and Peter Brötzmann, among others.

In the 1980s younger musicians joined the orchestra, such as the violinist Mary Oliver. Under Mengelberg's direction the ICP Orchestra studied and recorded the music of Duke Ellington, Herbie Nichols and Thelonious Monk. At the end of the 1980s a long collaboration with the Dutch punk group The Ex also began. The records from the first years appeared in 1970 and 1971, and later came East of the Sun in 2014, among others. The ICP made clear that free improvisation in the Netherlands had a playful tradition of its own, with humour, theatre and an open view of jazz history.
artiest/icp-orchestra.listen: Listen to a recording by the orchestra and notice the moment when a theme by Monk or Ellington becomes almost recognisable and then falls apart again. Who plays what, and when does someone choose precisely not to play anything?

artiest/igor-markevitch.text:
Igor Markevitch was a Russian composer and conductor. He was born on 27 July 1912 in Kyiv, grew up in France and Switzerland, and studied and worked in Paris. Later he became an Italian and French citizen. In 1929 the impresario Sergei Diaghilev commissioned a piano concerto from him and invited him to write a ballet with Boris Kochno. Diaghilev died that year, but the publisher Schott took Markevitch on anyway.

In the 1930s he wrote at least one major work every year and was called the second Igor, after Stravinsky. His ballets Rébus and L'Envol d'Icare were performed in concert form, the latter with quarter tones in the winds. In 1941 he became seriously ill. After that he gave up composing and chose conducting. He made his debut at eighteen with the Concertgebouw Orchestra, studied with Pierre Monteux and Hermann Scherchen, and during the war helped the Resistance in Italy.

After 1947 he lived in Switzerland and conducted all over the world, including the Orchestre Lamoureux in Paris, the orchestra of Spanish RTVE, the London Symphony Orchestra and the Monte Carlo Philharmonic. He was admired for his French, Russian and Austro-German repertoire and for twentieth-century music. His recordings from the 1950s and 1960s, such as The Rite of Spring and Symphonie fantastique, remain in circulation. From 1970 he also conducted his own work again. He died in 1983 in Antibes, after a tour of Japan and Russia.
artiest/igor-markevitch.listen: Listen to The Rite of Spring in his recording and notice the rhythmic sharpness: where do the accents fall, and how does the orchestra keep the tempo tight while the time signatures keep changing?

artiest/igor-stravinsky.text: Igor Stravinsky was a pupil of Rimsky-Korsakov and became famous in Paris with ballets for Sergei Diaghilev's Ballets Russes. In Le sacre du printemps from 1913, clashing chords and irregular, stamping rhythms drive on the story of a pagan sacrifice. The premiere ended in a famous uproar in the hall. Later he changed style twice more, first to neoclassicism and, in old age, to the twelve-tone technique.
artiest/igor-stravinsky.listen: Listen to Les augures printaniers (The Augurs of Spring) and hear how the strings keep stamping on one grating chord, with accents that always fall in unexpected places.

artiest/ike-en-tina-turner.text:
Ike & Tina Turner was an American duo of the married couple Ike and Tina Turner. From 1960 to 1976 they performed as the Ike & Tina Turner Revue, with Ike's band the Kings of Rhythm and three backing singers, the Ikettes. Ike Turner came from Clarksdale in Mississippi and had built up his band in the St. Louis region. There the young Anna Mae Bullock sang along with him. In 1960 she recorded A Fool In Love, written by Ike, because the intended singer failed to show up. The record became a hit on the rhythm and blues charts in July 1960, and Ike gave her the stage name Tina.

The success was followed by I Idolize You, It's Gonna Work Out Fine and Poor Fool. For years the troupe toured the United States and played for mixed audiences in the Deep South. In 1966 Phil Spector produced River Deep, Mountain High, a record that sold poorly in America but established their name in Europe, partly thanks to a tour with the Rolling Stones. Later they made soul versions of rock songs, such as Come Together and Honky Tonk Woman. Proud Mary earned a Grammy in 1972.

The music combined rhythm and blues, soul and rock with a tight horn section and elaborate dance routines. Ike and Tina were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1991. Behind the successful show lay a violent marriage. Tina left Ike in 1976, which ended the duo.
artiest/ike-en-tina-turner.listen: Listen to Proud Mary and notice how it is built: the song starts quietly and almost politely and then turns into a much faster version. What happens to Tina's voice and to the backing singers?

artiest/ike-turner.text:
Ike Turner was an American musician, bandleader, songwriter, producer and talent scout. He was born in 1931 in Clarksdale, Mississippi. As a boy he learned boogie-woogie at the piano from the blues pianist Pinetop Perkins, and as a teenager he started the Kings of Rhythm, a band that played blues and boogie-woogie. He got his knowledge of music from listening: he could not read notes.

In March 1951 the band recorded Rocket 88 in Memphis, in Sam Phillips's studio. The saxophonist Jackie Brenston sang and Turner played piano, while the distorted guitar of Willie Kizart stood out. The record was released under Brenston's name and became a big R&B hit. Turner himself later said that it was really R&B, but that it was nevertheless the cause of rock 'n' roll. After that he worked as a producer and talent scout for Sun and Modern, and played a part in the early careers of B.B. King, Howlin' Wolf and Bobby Bland. He also taught himself to play guitar. In 1960 he started the Ike & Tina Turner Revue with his wife Tina, with hits such as A Fool in Love, River Deep Mountain High, Proud Mary and Nutbush City Limits.

Turner is seen as one of the innovators of early rock 'n' roll, who brought the intensity of the blues into commercial music. His life was overshadowed by his cocaine addiction and the domestic violence that Tina Turner later described. At the end of his life he returned to the blues. He died in 2007.
artiest/ike-turner.listen: Listen to Rocket 88 (1951). Notice Turner's rolling piano, the saxophones and above all the distorted, raw sound of the guitar.

artiest/ilaiyaraaja.text: Ilaiyaraaja grew up in a village in Tamil Nadu and as a boy played in his brother's music group. Later he received a Western classical training. With his debut Annakkili (1976) he brought Tamil folk music into the cinema, combined with Western orchestration; later synthesizers and counterpoint were added. He wrote music for more than a thousand films in various South Indian languages. His collaboration with the director Mani Ratnam produced classics such as Mouna Ragam (1986), Nayakan (1987) and Thalapathi (1991). A generation of Indian composers, among them A.R. Rahman, began in his circle.
artiest/ilaiyaraaja.listen: Listen to the interplay between the singing voice and the countermelodies in the strings and flute, and to the folk rhythms on Indian drums.

artiest/illinois-jacquet.text:
Illinois Jacquet was an American jazz saxophonist, born on 30 October 1922. His parents were Creoles from Louisiana, but he grew up in Houston, Texas. His father led a band in his spare time and Illinois played alto in that group as a child. At fifteen he was already working with the Milton Larkin Orchestra, a dance band from the region. In 1939 he moved to Los Angeles, where Nat King Cole put him in touch with Lionel Hampton. Hampton wanted him in his new big band, but on tenor saxophone.

In 1942 Jacquet, nineteen years old, played the solo on Flying Home with Hampton's orchestra. It was one of the first times a screaming, raw tenor sax was heard on record. The piece became the climax of every concert, and later saxophonists copied the solo. After that he worked with Cab Calloway, appeared in the film Jammin' the Blues and took part in the first Jazz at the Philharmonic concert. In 1946 he succeeded Lester Young in Count Basie's orchestra. With Jimmy Mundy he wrote Black Velvet, which became a standard as Don'cha Go 'Way Mad.

Jacquet played with a hard sound that ranged high and low, but could also improvise melodically on ballads. As one of the few jazz musicians, he also played the bassoon. His style influenced the saxophone in rhythm and blues and rock 'n' roll. He also protested against segregation in his hometown of Houston. He kept performing until his death in 2004.
artiest/illinois-jacquet.listen: Listen to Flying Home with Lionel Hampton and notice the tenor solo: how does Jacquet use the lowest and highest notes, and how does he build tension before the band comes in?

artiest/ilse-delange.text:
Ilse DeLange is a Dutch singer and songwriter who makes country and pop rock. She was born on 13 May 1977 in Almelo. At the age of eight she began as a lip-sync performer and won competitions with it. Later she switched to singing live in talent contests and on television. In 1994 she performed at the Dutch Country Music Awards and took part in the Zangfestival der Onbekenden in Eindhoven.

In 1998 she travelled with the group Cash On Delivery to Nashville to record her debut album World of Hurt with the producer Barry Beckett. The fact that the album was recorded in the capital of country music drew a great deal of attention in the Netherlands. The single I'm Not So Tough reached the Top 40. A year later came the live album Dear John, full of covers of John Hiatt. Livin' on Love in 2000 sounded more like pop and rock, and on Clean Up from 2003 she wrote all the lyrics herself. In 2006 The Great Escape appeared on Universal, with The Lonely One and I Love You, among others.

In 2014 she sang with The Common Linnets at the Eurovision Song Contest, where the group came second. In 2019 she accompanied Duncan Laurence to victory with Arcade. She won several Edison Awards and the Jeff Walker Global Country Music Award. DeLange showed that Dutch country could reach an audience of its own, with warm vocals and guitars reminiscent of Nashville.
artiest/ilse-delange.listen: Listen to I'm Not So Tough and notice the way the voice and the guitars alternate. Which elements belong to country, and what sounds distinctly like Dutch pop?

artiest/imamyar-hasanov.text:
Imamyar Hasanov is an Azerbaijani musician known as a player of the kamancha, a round-bodied fiddle with a skin soundboard. He is regarded as one of the best-known kamancha players in his country. No further personal details are recorded in the available sources, so the text sticks to what is certain.

Together with the tar and the frame drum ghaval, the kamancha is the core of mugham, the classical music of Azerbaijan. Together these three instruments form a trio. The strings of the kamancha are traditionally made of silk or horsehair, and the sound is soft, nasal and highly expressive. Mugham consists largely of improvisation: within a given mode, such as Bayati Shiraz, the musician builds his own melody, with long ornamented phrases and free rhythms.

The 2007 recording, an improvisation on mugham Bayati Shiraz, shows that art. For the history of pop this music matters because it reveals a completely different approach to melody. The mode is not a sequence of chords but a collection of moods, and the player has to turn them into a story in the moment. Much later world music and fusion was inspired by such traditions.
artiest/imamyar-hasanov.listen: Listen to the improvisation on mugham Bayati Shiraz and notice how the melody floats freely through time, without a fixed rhythm, with long sweeping phrases and trills on the string.

artiest/imogen-heap.text:
Imogen Heap is an English singer, songwriter and producer. She was born on 9 December 1977 in Romford and had classical piano lessons. As a child she recorded herself on cassette: first the piano, then her singing on top. At sixteen she went to the BRIT School in south London. Her debut album I Megaphone appeared in 1998 on Almo Sounds, but sold poorly and she soon found herself without a record contract.

In 2000 she formed the electronic duo Frou Frou with the producer Guy Sigsworth. Their only album, Details, came out in 2002. The song Let Go became known through the film Garden State. After that she took matters into her own hands. Speak for Yourself from 2005 she wrote, produced, recorded and mixed entirely herself, and she released it on her own label Megaphonic Records. On that album she played almost all the instruments herself. Hide and Seek became known internationally after it was heard in the television series The O.C. Headlock, too, became popular again on TikTok in 2024.

Heap works with electropop, layers of voice and a great deal of studio technique. She developed the Mi.Mu gloves, gloves with which she controls music through gestures. She wrote the music for the stage play Harry Potter and the Cursed Child. In her own work she shows how a singer can also be a producer and inventor.
artiest/imogen-heap.listen: Listen to Hide and Seek and pay attention to the voice. The song is made of vocal layers. How do the harmonies sound, and what role do the electronic effects play?

artiest/incognito.text:
Incognito is a British band from London that counts as acid jazz. The group was founded around 1979 by Jean-Paul Bluey Maunick and Paul Tubbs Williams, as an offshoot of the funk band Light of the World. Maunick is the constant frontman: guitarist, singer, composer and producer. The debut album Jazz Funk appeared in 1981. The idea behind the group was a formation that combines jazz, soul and funk, with changing musicians and above all changing singers.

The breakthrough came in 1991 with Always There, an adaptation of a song by Ronnie Laws from 1975, sung by Jocelyn Brown. It was a hit in the United Kingdom and was also important for the label Talkin' Loud. In 1992 followed a version of Don't You Worry 'bout a Thing. In the Netherlands Always There reached the Top 40. Among the male and female singers who have worked with the band are Carleen Anderson, Maysa Leak, Imaani and Tony Momrelle. In 1994 the band contributed to the album Stolen Moments: Red Hot + Cool, which raised money to fight AIDS. The song Need to Know is the theme tune of the news programme Democracy Now!

Incognito's music sounds warm and danceable, with horns, tight bass lines and a supple vocal part. Remixers such as Masters at Work, David Morales and Jazzanova liked working with the material. In 2021 an expanded reissue of Jazz Funk appeared to mark the fortieth anniversary.
artiest/incognito.listen: Listen to Always There and notice the groove: what do the bass and horns do, and how does the voice fit in with them?

artiest/incredible-bongo-band.text:
The Incredible Bongo Band was an American studio project of the 1970s. It began in 1972 with Michael Viner, a manager and executive at MGM Records, together with Mike Curb and the arranger Perry Botkin Jr. Viner had to supply additional music for the B-movie The Thing With Two Heads. He used MGM's studio when it was free and gathered the musicians who happened to be there, among them Glen Campbell on guitar and Harry Nilsson on keyboards and for arrangements. Jim Gordon played drums, and Bobby Hall and King Erisson percussion.

The group released two albums: Bongo Rock in 1973 and Return of the Incredible Bongo Band in 1974. The first album contains an adaptation of Bongo Rock, a song by Preston Epps from 1959, and of Apache, an instrumental piece by Jerry Lordan that was earlier known from The Shadows. The Arrows took their version as a model. The music is instrumental, funky and built on bongos and congas.

The record went unnoticed for a long time, until hip hop pioneers such as DJ Kool Herc and Grandmaster Flash began to use the drums in the late 1970s. Last Bongo in Belgium was sampled by the Beastie Boys, Massive Attack and Leftfield, among others. In this way Apache became a building block of hip hop. Bongo Rock appears in the book 1001 Albums You Must Hear Before You Die, and Bongolia was heard in 2017 in the film Baby Driver.
artiest/incredible-bongo-band.listen: Listen to Apache and pay attention to the percussion: how do the bongos and drums together hold a rhythm that you could loop, and what do the guitar and horns do above it?

artiest/inner-city.text:
Inner City is the project of the Detroit producer Kevin Saunderson and the singer Paris Grey, formed in 1987. Saunderson was born in Brooklyn in 1964 and grew up in Belleville, a suburb of Detroit. With his school friends Juan Atkins and Derrick May he formed the Belleville Three, the group that stood at the cradle of Detroit techno. With Inner City, Saunderson showed that this new, machine-made music could also work as a pop song.

Big Fun began in 1987 as an instrumental track that Saunderson made while he was still studying. The Chicago house producer Terry Baldwin put him in touch with Paris Grey, who wrote the lyrics. Beneath her warm house vocals runs a tight, mechanical beat from the drum machine, with short synthesizer chords. In 1988 the track appeared on the British compilation Techno! The New Dance Sound of Detroit and in August of that year was released as a single on 10 Records. It reached number 8 in England and number 1 on the American dance chart. The follow-up Good Life reached number 4 in England. Both songs are on the album Paradise (1989), which reached number 3 in England.

Inner City was the commercial side of Detroit techno. Where Atkins and May made music mainly for DJs and clubs, Saunderson scored in the hit parade. Under other names he also kept making club records, such as Reese and E-Dancer. The grating, floating bass line of Just Want Another Chance (1988), released as Reese, was imitated so often in jungle and drum and bass in the 1990s that this sound is called the Reese bass.
artiest/inner-city.listen: In Big Fun, notice the contrast between the voice and the machine: Paris Grey sings smoothly and warmly like a house singer, while the beat beneath stays stiff and angular, with short bursts of synthesizer chords. That is techno from Detroit with a pop singer from the Chicago area on top.

artiest/inspiral-carpets.text:
Inspiral Carpets is an English rock band from Oldham, near Manchester. The guitarist Graham Lambert and the singer Stephen Holt, friends from school, started the group in 1983 as a garage and punk band. In 1986 the fourteen-year-old drummer Craig Gill joined, and later the keyboard player Clint Boon. When Holt left, he was replaced by Tom Hingley. With Hingley, Gill, Lambert, Boon and the bassist Martyn Walsh the band had its most successful line-up.

The band became known in the late 1980s in the Madchester scene, together with the Stone Roses and Happy Mondays. The DJ John Peel often played the Planecrash EP (1988) and asked the band for a session. Because their distributor went bankrupt, they started their own label, Cow Records. They then signed to Mute and had success with This Is How It Feels and the debut album Life (1990). There followed The Beast Inside (1991), Revenge of the Goldfish (1992) and Devil Hopping (1994), with Saturn 5 and I Want You, which they recorded with Mark E. Smith. In 1995 the group broke up. Later they reunited a few times, and in 2014 the album Inspiral Carpets appeared.

The band's sound revolved around Clint Boon's organ and distorted guitars, with influences from the psychedelic rock of the 1960s. One of the band's roadies would later become more famous than the group itself: Noel Gallagher worked for them as a drum technician before he went on to play with Oasis.
artiest/inspiral-carpets.listen: Listen to This Is How It Feels (1990). Notice Clint Boon's organ, which is almost as important as the guitar, and how that organ brings back the atmosphere of the 1960s.

artiest/instant-composers-pool.text:
The Instant Composers Pool, abbreviated ICP, is an independent Dutch label and orchestra for jazz and improvised music. It was founded in Amsterdam in 1967 by the saxophonist Willem Breuker, the pianist Misha Mengelberg and the drummer Han Bennink. The name comes from the idea that improvisation amounts to composing in the moment itself. As European free jazz players, the three musicians met with little interest from established labels and therefore built a cooperative to release their own recordings.

The label's first release, a record by Breuker and Bennink, appeared in 1967. In 1968 followed Instant Composers Pool with Mengelberg, Bennink and John Tchicai. In the 1970s records also came out by Derek Bailey, Steve Lacy, Evan Parker, Dudu Pukwana and Peter Brötzmann, often as coproductions with other European independent labels. Breuker left in 1974 and started his own label BVHaast. Mengelberg and Bennink carried on.

In the 1980s younger musicians joined the orchestra, among them the violinist Mary Oliver. The ICP Orchestra played and recorded music by Duke Ellington, Herbie Nichols and Thelonious Monk. Later it worked with members of Sonic Youth and with the Dutch punk group The Ex. The label released more than fifty titles. In 2012, to mark the forty-fifth anniversary, the entire catalogue appeared in a box of fifty-four CDs. The ICP showed that a small, independent organisation could build a musical world of its own.
artiest/instant-composers-pool.listen: Listen to a recording of the ICP Orchestra with music by Thelonious Monk and notice the places where the theme is briefly recognisable. Who takes it over, and how does the conversation between the instruments sound?

artiest/international-sweethearts-of-rhy.text:
The International Sweethearts of Rhythm were an American jazz orchestra and are regarded as the first racially integrated all-women big band in the United States. The first members met in 1938 at the Piney Woods Country Life School in Mississippi, a school for poor and Black children, where many pupils were orphans. The bandleader was at first the school's founder and director, Laurence C. Jones. In 1941 the women continued as a professional orchestra and broke with the school. They settled in Arlington, Virginia.

The members came from varied backgrounds, including Latina, Asian, white, Black and Native American, and that gave the band its international name. Eddie Durham wrote the first arrangements, Jesse Stone took over in 1941 and brought in experienced musicians to help the younger players. The orchestra played swing and jazz in theatres such as the Apollo in New York, the Regal in Chicago and the Howard in Washington. In 1941 they set a box-office record at the Howard with thirty-five thousand visitors in a week. They also made short films for cinemas. Because of the racial laws of the South they lived partly on their bus.

In 1944 DownBeat magazine named them the best women's orchestra in America. Maurice King led the orchestra after Stone, and in 1948 they played together with Dizzy Gillespie. The band showed that women could lead a top-level big band, and was later rediscovered when Marian McPartland brought them to a festival of women jazz musicians in 1980.
artiest/international-sweethearts-of-rhy.listen: Listen to a recording of the orchestra and notice the horn section: how tightly does the group play together, and how do soloists stand out against the arrangement?

artiest/iola-brubeck.text:
Iola Brubeck was an American lyricist and the wife of the jazz pianist Dave Brubeck. She met him at the College of the Pacific in California and married him in 1942. Dave Brubeck became known with his quartet and the record Time Out (1959), with music in unusual time signatures. Iola worked behind the scenes on that career. She wrote lyrics to her husband's compositions and helped organise the quartet's performances at American universities, through which the group reached a new, young audience.

Her best-known work is The Real Ambassadors, a jazz musical that she and Dave made in 1961. The piece was partly based on what she and their colleagues experienced on foreign tours for the American State Department. Brubeck's quartet had made such a tour in 1958, with concerts in Poland, Turkey, India and Iran, among other places. On the record Louis Armstrong, the vocal trio Lambert, Hendricks & Ross and Carmen McRae sing. In 1962 the musical was performed at the Monterey Jazz Festival.

The Real Ambassadors looks with humour and criticism at jazz as America's calling card. Musicians who faced racial segregation at home had to carry their country's freedom abroad. With her lyrics Iola Brubeck gave that contradiction a voice.
artiest/iola-brubeck.listen: Listen to the title song of The Real Ambassadors (1961), sung by Louis Armstrong. Notice how the lyric is about jazz musicians as ambassadors, and how Armstrong delivers those words in his warm, raw voice.

artiest/iq.text:
IQ is a British neo-prog band, founded in 1981 by Mike Holmes and Martin Orford, after the break-up of their earlier band The Lens. From 1982 the line-up consisted of the singer Peter Nicholls, the guitarist Mike Holmes, the keyboard player Martin Orford, the drummer Paul Cook and the bassist Tim Esau. Nicholls also drew the sleeves of most of the albums on which he appears. In 1985 he left briefly to start another band and was replaced by Paul Menel, but in 1990 he returned.

IQ belongs to a wave of British groups from the early 1980s, such as Marillion, Pendragon, Twelfth Night and Pallas, who continued the progressive rock that Genesis and Yes had left behind in the 1970s. The music press later called this neo-prog. Orford thought that term unjustified and pointed out that the band had many different influences. The group never had major commercial successes, but built up a loyal fan base and is still active. In 2021 and 2022 it celebrated its fortieth anniversary with concerts in the United Kingdom and Europe.

The music is characterised by long songs, a large share of keyboards and guitar, and almost theatrical vocals. Especially in the early years the group sounded like Genesis. For the history of pop, IQ matters above all as proof that progressive rock continued to exist after punk, among a loyal audience and outside the charts.
artiest/iq.listen: Listen to The Wake and notice the long build-up with keyboard parts and guitar solos: how does the mood change over the course of the song, and can you hear the influence of Genesis?

artiest/ira-gershwin.text:
Ira Gershwin was an American lyricist. He was born on 6 December 1896 as Israel Gershovitz, the eldest son of Russian-Jewish immigrants in Manhattan. The family lived in the middle of the Yiddish theatre district. While his younger brother George was already working in Tin Pan Alley at eighteen, Ira was a cashier at his father's Turkish baths. He was shy, read a great deal and wrote for school newspapers. His first published lyric was a parody in 1917. To stay separate from George, he wrote under the name Arthur Francis.

In 1924 came the brothers' first Broadway hit, Lady, Be Good. Together they made thirteen musicals and wrote songs such as I Got Rhythm, Embraceable You and The Man I Love. After Porgy and Bess, which was a commercial disappointment, they went to Hollywood for films such as Shall We Dance and A Damsel in Distress. In 1937 George died suddenly of a brain tumour. Ira waited almost three years before he wrote again, and then worked with composers such as Kurt Weill, Jerome Kern and Harold Arlen.

His lyrics are playful, precise and close to spoken language. Ira was able to follow a melody by George so closely that word and note became one whole. The success of the duo often overshadowed his own share, but his book Lyrics on Several Occasions from 1959, a mixture of autobiography and commentary, was well received. He died in 1983.
artiest/ira-gershwin.listen: Listen to I Got Rhythm and notice the lyric: how does the language adapt to the rhythm of the melody, and which rhymes stand out?

artiest/irene-cara.text:
Irene Cara was an American singer and actress. She was born on 18 March 1959 in the Bronx in New York, the youngest of five children. Her father was Puerto Rican and her mother Cuban. She took dance lessons from an early age. In 1971 she was part of the band Short Circus on the educational programme The Electric Company, and as a child she recorded a Spanish-language record and a Christmas album. She appeared on Broadway and off-Broadway in Via Galactica, Ain't Misbehavin' and The Me Nobody Knows, among others. In 1976 she played the title role in the film Sparkle.

The breakthrough came in 1980 with the film Fame by Alan Parker. She was cast as a dancer, but the producers heard her voice and rewrote the role of Coco Hernandez for her. She sang the title song Fame and Out Here on My Own. In 1983 she wrote Flashdance... What a Feeling, the title song of the film Flashdance, together with Giorgio Moroder and Keith Forsey. In 1984 came Breakdance, her last Top 40 hit. Her albums were Anyone Can See in 1982, What a Feelin' in 1983 and Carasmatic in 1987.

Her music combined pop and dance with the synthesizers of the early 1980s. She showed how film music and pop music came together in that era: her hits were soundtrack songs, and the film brought the record to a large audience. Irene Cara died in 2022.
artiest/irene-cara.listen: Listen to Flashdance... What a Feeling and notice how it is built: how does the song begin, and what do the synthesizers and the drum machine do once the beat sets in?

artiest/irene-schweizer.text: The pianist Irène Schweizer from Schaffhausen in Switzerland first played Dixieland and hard bop, and in the 1960s became one of the first European women in free jazz. In 1967 she played on Jazz Meets India. She worked with Peter Brötzmann, Louis Moholo and Han Bennink, and in the 1970s also with the Feminist Improvising Group, a group of improvising women. From 1986 she recorded extensively for the Zürich label Intakt, which she co-founded. Her playing is energetic and rhythmic, with influences from South African jazz that she heard in Zürich in the 1960s. She died in 2024.
artiest/irene-schweizer.listen: Notice the rhythmic, almost dancing piano playing.

artiest/iron-maiden.text:
Iron Maiden is an English heavy metal band, founded in 1975 in Leyton in east London by the bassist Steve Harris. He wrote most of the songs. The name came from an instrument of torture, the iron maiden. After many changes in the line-up, the band found the singer Paul Di'Anno in 1978. A demo that a DJ played in a London metal club quickly made Iron Maiden known. The band released those recordings themselves as The Soundhouse Tapes, and the pressing sold out within a few weeks.

With the albums Iron Maiden (1980) and Killers (1981) the group became a pioneer of the New Wave of British Heavy Metal, the wave of new British metal bands around 1980. In 1981 Bruce Dickinson replaced Di'Anno as singer. His first album with the band, The Number of the Beast (1982), which includes Run to the Hills, became one of the most popular metal albums ever. Iron Maiden's sound revolves around Harris's fast, galloping bass lines, two guitarists playing melodies together and Dickinson's high, powerful voice. The lyrics are about history, war, mythology, literature and science fiction.

On almost every sleeve appears the mascot Eddie, a monstrous figure who also appears on stage. After a difficult period in the 1990s, Dickinson and the guitarist Adrian Smith returned in 1999, and the band then grew again. Iron Maiden is regarded as one of the most influential metal bands and was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2026.
artiest/iron-maiden.listen: Listen to Run to the Hills and notice the galloping rhythm of bass and drums, like a horse at a trot. Hear how the two guitars play the melody together and how Bruce Dickinson wails high in the chorus.
